description_full: TIM S.A. engages in the telecommunications sector in Brazil. It offers landline switched telephone services in local, national, and international long-distance modes, as well as personal mobile and multimedia communication services. The company is based in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. TIM S.A. is a subsidiary of TIM Brasil Serviços e Participações S.A.
ceo_bio: Mr. Alberto Mario Griselli | President, CEO & Director | Age 56
financial_summary: TIM S.A. is a mid-cap communication services business with a $8.6B market cap on $4.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 16% against a 8% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 53% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.6B in free cash flow — roughly 33 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.12× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -16.0% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.9× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 6.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 24% operating margin runs 15pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.16x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 169 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 16% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 36% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.53, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.32 vs 5y 0.38), so read it loosely.
About $10.5M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.9x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash, 28% in the 2022 bear market and 73% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 83% below its DCF fair value of $108, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $77.70 to $155 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Communication Services peers: P/E 10.7 vs 14.9, EV/EBITDA 1.8 vs 9.4 and P/FCF 5.3 vs 11.3 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-2%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 18.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $23.35 on average, 29% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 7.8% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.31).
It runs a 53% gross margin and converts 33% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 3.12x, but high accruals (-16.0% of assets).
ROE of 18% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $151.1M.
The current ratio of 0.89 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.5% over 3 years and 7.1% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.2% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 5.3% on average.
Analysts expect 12.6% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 5%.
It returns 6.5% a year to shareholders (8.7% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 27 consecutive years, raising it 21.2% a year over the last five.
